docs.title: Establishing Quantified Uncertainty in Neural Networks
Usage
docs.text:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) for supervised labeling problems are known to produce accurate results on a wide variety of learning tasks. However, when accuracy is the only objective, DNNs frequently make over-confident predictions, and they also always make a label prediction regardless of whether or not the test data belongs to any known labels.

EQUINE was created to simplify two kinds of uncertainty quantification for supervised labeling problems: 1) Calibrated probabilities for each predicted label 2) An in-distribution score, indicating whether any of the model's known labels should be trusted. Additionally, we provide a companion web application.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Users are recommended to install a virtual environment such as Anaconda, as is also recommended in the pytorch installation. EQUINE has relatively few dependencies beyond torch. 

pip install equine
EQUINE supports Python 3.11 to 3.15 and requires torch 2.14.1 or later (on macOS, an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 14 or later). On Python 3.15, install torch from PyTorch's index first: 
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
pip install equine
On macOS with Python 3.15, use torch 2.15 or later: torch 2.14 crashes there when it is used from several threads at once, and EQUINE warns at import. Until torch 2.15 is released, install it from PyTorch's test index: 
pip install --upgrade 'torch>=2.15' --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu
Users interested in contributing should refer to CONTRIBUTING.md for details.

docs.title: Design
docs.text: EQUINE extends pytorch's nn.Module interface using a predict method that returns both the class predictions and the extra OOD scores.

docs.title: Developer Installation
docs.text:
1. Clone the git repository and navigate to that directory

  2. Install a virtual environment. We currently support python versions from 3.11 to 3.15.

    Using conda:

    conda create --name equine python==3.11
conda activate equine

    Or, alternatively, using uv:

    uv venv --python 3.11
source .venv/bin/activate

  3. Install the code with the dev extra (the test dependencies plus pre-commit and codespell)

    pip install -e .'[dev]'

    If you created the environment with uv, you can use uv pip instead:

    uv pip install -e '.[dev]'

    On Python 3.15, torch is published only on PyTorch's own package index until torch 2.15 reaches PyPI; install it from there first, e.g. pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu. On macOS with Python 3.15, use torch >= 2.15 (torch 2.14 crashes there when used from several threads, and EQUINE warns at import); until it is released, use https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu, or for tox EQUINE_TORCH_INDEX=https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu tox -r -e py315 (-r rebuilds an environment that already has an older torch).

  4. Activate the pre-commit hooks 

    pre-commit install
pre-commit run

  5. For local testing, install tox (pip install tox).

    Optionally, also install tox-uv (pip install tox tox-uv) to have tox use uv to build its environments and install dependencies. This is drop-in (no tox config changes) and significantly faster — it's the same backend CI uses.

We prefer that any contributed code be outfitted with contracts from icontract and tested with hypothesis. This combination frequently means that the tests require few (if any) actual post-checks -- if the contracts are well-written, then hypothesis can generate reasonable tests that will explore the bounds of the contracts for each method. Assuming that tests pass, then make a pull request.

docs.title: Continuous Integration
docs.text: There are a number of Github Actions enabled to ensure high code quality upon commiting. * Tests must be added and all tests must pass (100%) before closing a pull request * Total coverage should be 97% or higher * We enforce a code style via ruff (formatting + linting, including import sorting) and codespell. If formatting issues are found, tox -e format usually fixes them automatically. * A job runs the suite with every dependency at the lowest version pyproject.toml allows (tox -e floors, which needs tox-uv). When code needs a newer release of a dependency, raise its floor.

class LeNet(torch.nn.Module):

    def __init__(self):
        super(LeNet, self).__init__()
        self.conv1 = torch.nn.Conv2d(1, 6, 5, padding=2)
        self.conv2 = torch.nn.Conv2d(6, 16, 5)
        self.fc1   = torch.nn.Linear(16*5*5, 120)
        self.fc2   = torch.nn.Linear(120, 84)
        self.fc3   = torch.nn.Linear(84, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv1(x)), (2, 2))
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv2(x)), (2, 2))
        x = x.view(-1, self.num_flat_features(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
        x = self.fc3(x)
        return x

    def num_flat_features(self, x):
        size = x.size()[1:]
        return torch.prod(torch.tensor(size))

@eq.embedding_architecture("examples.lenet_embedding")
class EmbeddingModel(LeNet):

    # the weights of the layers named in `frozen` (e.g. "conv1") are
    # not updated during training
    def __init__(self, frozen=()):
        super(EmbeddingModel, self).__init__()
        for name in frozen:
            self.get_submodule(name).weight.requires_grad = False


def pretrained_embedding(source, frozen):
    """A new EmbeddingModel whose `frozen` layers have the weights learned by `source`."""
    embedding = EmbeddingModel(frozen=frozen)
    with torch.no_grad():
        for name in frozen:
            embedding.get_submodule(name).weight.copy_(source.get_submodule(name).weight)
    return embedding
class LeNet(torch.nn.Module): def __init__(self): super(LeNet, self).__init__() self.conv1 = torch.nn.Conv2d(1, 6, 5, padding=2) self.conv2 = torch.nn.Conv2d(6, 16, 5) self.fc1 = torch.nn.Linear(16*5*5, 120) self.fc2 = torch.nn.Linear(120, 84) self.fc3 = torch.nn.Linear(84, 10) def forward(self, x): x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv1(x)), (2, 2)) x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv2(x)), (2, 2)) x = x.view(-1, self.num_flat_features(x)) x = F.relu(self.fc1(x)) x = F.relu(self.fc2(x)) x = self.fc3(x) return x def num_flat_features(self, x): size = x.size()[1:] return torch.prod(torch.tensor(size)) @eq.embedding_architecture("examples.lenet_embedding") class EmbeddingModel(LeNet): # the weights of the layers named in `frozen` (e.g. "conv1") are # not updated during training def __init__(self, frozen=()): super(EmbeddingModel, self).__init__() for name in frozen: self.get_submodule(name).weight.requires_grad = False def pretrained_embedding(source, frozen): """A new EmbeddingModel whose `frozen` layers have the weights learned by `source`.""" embedding = EmbeddingModel(frozen=frozen) with torch.no_grad(): for name in frozen: embedding.get_submodule(name).weight.copy_(source.get_submodule(name).weight) return embedding

We train the model for 30 epochs using SGD with two scheduled drops in learning rate.

loss_fn = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
opt = torch.optim.SGD(
        model_orig.parameters(),
        lr=0.01,
        momentum=0.9,
        weight_decay=0.0001,
    )
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.MultiStepLR(opt, milestones=[20,25], gamma=0.1)

for epoch in range(30):
    epoch_loss = 0.0
    for i, (xs, labels) in enumerate(trainloader):
        opt.zero_grad()
        yhats = model_orig(xs)
        loss = loss_fn(yhats, labels)
        batch_acc = train_accuracy(yhats, labels)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
        epoch_loss += loss.item()
    #print(epoch_loss)
    total_train_accuracy = train_accuracy.compute()
    scheduler.step()

    print("Training acc for epoch {}: {:.3f}".format(epoch, total_train_accuracy))

To evaluate the model, we first consider its accuracy on the test dataset and then look at how well its predictive probabilities allow us to separate in-distribution data from out-of-distribution (OOD) data. To do this, we compute the entropy of the predictive probability distribution. Ideally, the model will produce predictions with low entropy for in distribution data and predictions with high entropy for out of distribution data.

In [7]: Copied! 
model_orig.eval()

oods_in_dist = []
predictions = []
true_labels = []
for i, (xs, labels) in enumerate(testloader):
    y_pred = model_orig(xs).detach().numpy()
    oods = np.sum(scipy.special.entr(scipy.special.softmax(y_pred, axis=1)), axis=1)
    oods_in_dist.extend(list(oods))
    predictions.extend(list(np.argmax(y_pred, axis=1)))
    true_labels.extend(list(labels))
predictions = np.array(predictions)
true_labels = np.array(true_labels)
print('Model accuracy on test set: {:.3f}'.format(np.mean(predictions == true_labels)))
    
oods_out_dist = []
for i, (xs, labels) in enumerate(oodloader):
    y_pred = model_orig(xs).detach().numpy()
    oods = np.sum(scipy.special.entr(scipy.special.softmax(y_pred, axis=1)), axis=1)
    oods_out_dist.extend(list(oods))
    
plt.hist(oods_in_dist,bins=np.linspace(0,3,61),alpha=0.5, label='In Distribution')
plt.hist(oods_out_dist,bins=np.linspace(0,3,61),alpha=0.5, label='Out of Distribution')
plt.xlabel('Entropy')
plt.ylabel('Count')
plt.legend()
plt.show()
roc = roc_auc_score(np.hstack((np.ones_like(oods_out_dist),np.zeros_like(oods_in_dist))),
              oods_out_dist+oods_in_dist)
print('AUROC for detecting out of distribution examples: {:.3f}'.format(roc))

Seeing the limitations of the original model, we will now freeze all but the output layer and wrap the model with two different equine models.

                      label_names=["T-shirt/top","Trouser","Pullover","Dress","Coat","Sandal","Shirt","Sneaker","Bag","Ankle boot"] )

Model accuracy on test set: 0.898

AUROC for detecting out of distribution examples: 0.865

The EquineGP model clearly does a much better job of separating the in distribution and out of distribution data. Returning to the digit 7 below, the original model put all of its probability on one class. How the EquineGP model scores a single example depends on training: in the run saved here, it is also confident about this digit and gives it a low out of distribution score, while other training runs (with other seeds, platforms or library versions) usually give it lower confidence and a higher score. The AUROC above, computed over all of the test and out of distribution data, is the better measure of how well the model separates the two. The EquineGP out of distribution score is the entropy of the probabilities scaled to between 0 and 1 and is computed internally.

The protonet also does a good job of separating in distribution and out of distribution data, though its accuracy is lower than the original model for the Gaussian Process model. The OOD score produced by the protonet is based on the distance to a representation of the closest class, rather than on the entropy of predictive probabilities. One minus the OOD score of a particular example can be interpreted as the probability of observing an in distribution example that is further from its closest class representation than the example point. As a result, the ood scores for the in distribution data roughly follow a uniform distribution.

Below, we see that the out out of distribution example receives a high OOD score.

docs.title: EQUINE Image Classification Example¶
docs.text:
This notebook walks through a simple application of a Neural Network trained on a vision task -- predicting a clothing article in the FashionMNIST dataset -- as applied to image data from that and from regular MNIST, a handwritten digit dataset. In this, we load the datasets, train a model, wrap the model with two EQUINE architectures, and demonstrate out-of-distribution performance.

This notebook requires some extra dependencies to run. You can uncomment the below cell to install them into your local environment.

docs.title: 2. Create Embedding Model¶
docs.text: We define a simple CNN using the LeNet architecture and our embedding model, which can freeze chosen layers so that they are not updated during training. The class is registered with @eq.embedding_architecture, because model.save() stores an embedding model as the name of a registered architecture plus its plain-valued constructor arguments and weights (rather than as executable code), and refuses a class that is not registered. So its constructor takes the names of the layers to freeze, and the learned weights are copied in after construction.

docs.title: 3. Wrap embedding model with EquineGP¶
docs.text: We first create a new EmbeddingModel whose first four layers are frozen at the weights that we learned above. We then wrap that EmbeddingModel in EquineGP. The resulting model has an extra Gaussian Process "layer" on top of the original model.

docs.title: 4. Wrap embedding model with EquineProtonet¶
docs.text: Our second wrapper replaces the softmax output of the original model with a protonet.

@eq.embedding_architecture("examples.toy_mlp")
class ToyMLP(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_features: int, hidden: int, layers: int, out_features: int | None = None):
        super(ToyMLP, self).__init__()
        # `layers` blocks of Linear + ReLU, then an output layer if `out_features` is given
        stack = []
        width = in_features
        for _ in range(layers):
            stack += [torch.nn.Linear(width, hidden), torch.nn.ReLU()]
            width = hidden
        if out_features is not None:
            stack.append(torch.nn.Linear(hidden, out_features))
        self.linear_relu_stack = torch.nn.Sequential(*stack)

    def forward(self, x):
        logits = self.linear_relu_stack(x)
        return logits

# Note that we have left off the very last step (the softmax),
# so we'll need to apply that after the model to calculate "probabilities"
@eq.embedding_architecture("examples.toy_mlp") class ToyMLP(torch.nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_features: int, hidden: int, layers: int, out_features: int | None = None): super(ToyMLP, self).__init__() # `layers` blocks of Linear + ReLU, then an output layer if `out_features` is given stack = [] width = in_features for _ in range(layers): stack += [torch.nn.Linear(width, hidden), torch.nn.ReLU()] width = hidden if out_features is not None: stack.append(torch.nn.Linear(hidden, out_features)) self.linear_relu_stack = torch.nn.Sequential(*stack) def forward(self, x): logits = self.linear_relu_stack(x) return logits # Note that we have left off the very last step (the softmax), # so we'll need to apply that after the model to calculate "probabilities"

Before we test the results, here are a few helper functions for printing out metrics like:

  • Accuracy
  • Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Closest to zero is better, implying the NN output probabilities are well calibrated
  • Brier score, lower is better
  • Brier skill score, as compared to random guessing. Closer to 1.0 is better We also evaluate the NN on a 2-D mesh and plot a contour map of background confidences

def display_2d_test_and_confidence(y_hat, x_test, y_test, Xt, Yt, confidences, title_in=None, num_classes=4):
    """
    Print out accuracy, expected calibration error, and render a 2-D plot

    :param y_hat: NN predictions on test data
    :param x_test: X data for testing
    :param y_test: one-hot encoded ground truth labels
    :param Xt: meshgrid of x locations
    :param Yt: meshgrid of y locations
    :param confidences: 2D torch tensor of confidences (scores between 0 and 1)
    :param title_in: Optional title for plot
    """
    # Plot class confidences on countourf and overlay test data predictions 
    y_out = torch.argmax(y_hat,1)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    cf = ax.contourf(Xt.numpy(), Yt.numpy(), torch.reshape(confidences, [len(Xt),len(Yt)]), cmap=plt.cm.bone)
    fig.colorbar(cf, ax=ax)
    wrong_xs = torch.Tensor()
    markers = ["1", "+", ".", "o"] # 4-class default
    if num_classes == 5:
        markers = ["1", "+", ".", "o", "2"] 
    for class_i, marker in enumerate(markers):
        xs = x_test[(y_out == class_i) & (y_test == class_i)]
        wxs = x_test[(y_out == class_i) & (y_test != class_i)]
        wrong_xs = torch.cat((wrong_xs, wxs),0)
        ax.scatter(xs[:,0], xs[:,1],marker=marker,label=f'Class {class_i}')
    ax.scatter(wrong_xs[:,0], wrong_xs[:,1], marker="x", label="Incorrect")
    ax.legend()

    title = title_in
    if not title_in:
        title = "NN Test Predictions and Class Confidence"
    plt.title(title)


def print_metrics(y_hat, y_test, num_classes=4):
    """
    Print out accuracy, expected calibration error, and render a 2-D plot

    :param y_hat: NN predictions on test data
    :param y_test: one-hot encoded ground truth labels
    :param confidences: 2D torch tensor of confidences (scores between 0 and 1)
    """
    # Compute accuracy and ECE
    accuracy = Accuracy(task="multiclass", num_classes=num_classes, top_k=1)

    y_out = torch.argmax(y_hat,1)
    acc = accuracy(y_out, y_test)
    print(f"NN accuracy is {acc:3.2f}")
    
    ece = expected_calibration_error(y_hat, y_test)
    print(f"NN ECE is: {ece:3.2e}")
 
    bs = brier_score(y_hat, y_test)
    print(f"Brier score is: {bs:3.2e}")

    bss = brier_skill_score(y_hat, y_test)
    print(f"Brier skill score is: {bss:3.2f}")

# Pull out the feature embedding: the same layers without the last (output) one,
# built with the registered ToyMLP so that model.save() can store it, and
# initialized with the trained weights
embedding_model = ToyMLP(tensor_dim, hidden=16, layers=3)

    vanilla_nn.linear_relu_stack[:-1].state_dict())

# Create the EQUINE model, support examples, and pointers to those examples

docs.title: EQUINE Protonet Toy Problem Example¶
docs.text:
The intent of this example notebook is to provide an easy-to-visualize, 2-D, toy problem that illustrates both the general problem of uncertainty quantification in neural network classification as well as to show how EQUINE can be used to make predictions more robust in the face of uncertainty. Here, we use the EquineProtonet class to demonstrate the ideas, which appends an extra layer to a provided neural network embedding model and trains on distances to average class representations (prototypes) in the same way that protonets do, with the exception that we also add an out-of-distribution score.

This notebook requires some extra dependencies to run. You can uncomment the below cell to install them into your local environment.

docs.title: Generate Toy Dataset¶
docs.text:
This dataset uses make_blobs from scikit-learn, placing 4 clusters in each quadrant (for 4 classes), along with a middle cluster with random class memberships.

In this toy problem, the accuracy should not be much higher than 80%, since the middle class memberships are essentially random.

Additionally, the class confidence in the middle of the problem should hover around 25% for the same reason.

docs.title: Define our embedding model¶
docs.text:
Here we define a "usual" neural network architecture, leaving off only the softmax in the forward function.

The class is registered with @eq.embedding_architecture, because model.save() stores an embedding model as the name of a registered architecture plus its plain-valued constructor arguments and weights (rather than as executable code), and refuses a class that is not registered.

docs.title: Wrap the model using EQUINE¶
docs.text: In order to have more reliable confidence overlays, and to have any chance of estimating an out-of-distribution score for each inference, we need to evaluate distances in the penultimate layer of the network. EQUINE provides a way to take an existing model and data, add layer(s) for distance embedding, and output new quantities for uncertainty quantification.

docs.title: Retrain or fine-tune EQUINE model with episodic training¶
docs.text: To train a model, we use train_episodes, which has options explained below.

docs.title: Evaluate the results¶
docs.text:
EQUINE introduces the "predict()" API to return predictions with the probability contexts, including

  • classes: the class probabilities
  • ood_scores: the out-of-distribution scores as well as other variables

docs.title: Adding Out-Of-Distribution Data¶
docs.text: In this section, we add a new cluster of data just to the right of the existing data to showcase how one could use the "ood_score" attribute of EquineOutput.

docs.title: Bonus Protonet result (few-shot learning)¶
docs.text: Protonets are able to add additional classes without retraining! We next show how the OOD scores and confidences change when this happens. In the below cells, we generate some new "support" examples by randomly sampling 30 examples of each class, including the new class, and then using that to update the EquineProtonet model.

@eq.embedding_architecture("examples.toy_mlp")
class ToyMLP(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_features: int, hidden: int, layers: int, out_features: int | None = None):
        super(ToyMLP, self).__init__()
        # `layers` blocks of Linear + ReLU, then an output layer if `out_features` is given
        stack = []
        width = in_features
        for _ in range(layers):
            stack += [torch.nn.Linear(width, hidden), torch.nn.ReLU()]
            width = hidden
        if out_features is not None:
            stack.append(torch.nn.Linear(hidden, out_features))
        self.linear_relu_stack = torch.nn.Sequential(*stack)

    def forward(self, x):
        logits = self.linear_relu_stack(x)
        return logits

# Note that we have left off the very last step (the softmax),
# so we'll need to apply that after the model to calculate "probabilities"

Before we test the results, here are a few helper functions for printing out metrics like:

  • Accuracy
  • Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Closest to zero is better, implying well-calibrated NN output probabilities
  • Brier score, lower is better
  • Brier skill score, as compared to random guessing (closer to 1.0 is better)

We also evaluate the NN on a 2-D mesh and plot a contour map of background confidences.

def display_2d_test_and_confidence(y_hat, x_test, y_test, Xt, Yt, confidences, title_in=None):
    """
    Display test points as a scatter plot against a contour plot of confidence values

    :param y_hat: NN predictions on test data
    :param x_test: X data for testing
    :param y_test: one-hot encoded ground truth labels
    :param Xt: meshgrid of Cartesian X locations for contour plot
    :param Yt: meshgrid of Cartesian Y locations for contour plot
    :param confidences: 2D torch tensor of confidences (scores between 0 and 1)
    :param title_in: Optional title for plot
    """
    # Plot class confidences on countourf and overlay test data predictions 
    y_out = torch.argmax(y_hat,1)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    cf = ax.contourf(Xt.numpy(), Yt.numpy(), torch.reshape(confidences, [len(Xt),len(Yt)]), cmap=plt.cm.bone)
    fig.colorbar(cf, ax=ax)
    wrong_xs = torch.Tensor()
    for class_i, marker in enumerate(["1", "+", ".", "o"]):
        xs = x_test[(y_out == class_i) & (y_test == class_i)]
        wxs = x_test[(y_out == class_i) & (y_test != class_i)]
        wrong_xs = torch.cat((wrong_xs, wxs),0)
        ax.scatter(xs[:,0], xs[:,1],marker=marker,label=f'Class {class_i}')
    ax.scatter(wrong_xs[:,0], wrong_xs[:,1], marker="x", label="Incorrect")
    ax.legend()

    title = title_in
    if not title_in:
        title = "NN Test Predictions and Class Confidence"
    plt.title(title)


def print_metrics(y_hat, y_test, num_classes=4):
    """
    Print out accuracy, expected calibration error, and render a 2-D plot

    :param y_hat: NN predictions on test data
    :param y_test: one-hot encoded ground truth labels
    :param confidences: 2D torch tensor of confidences (scores between 0 and 1)
    """
    # Compute accuracy and ECE
    accuracy = Accuracy(task="multiclass", num_classes=num_classes, top_k=1)

    y_out = torch.argmax(y_hat,1)
    acc = accuracy(y_out, y_test)
    print(f"NN accuracy is {acc:3.2f}")
    
    ece = expected_calibration_error(y_hat, y_test)
    print(f"NN ECE is: {ece:3.2e}")
 
    bs = brier_score(y_hat, y_test)
    print(f"Brier score is: {bs:3.2e}")

    bss = brier_skill_score(y_hat, y_test)
    print(f"Brier skill score is: {bss:3.2f}")

After wrapping with EQUINE, the class confidences drop toward 25% (a random guess) between the input training clusters along the axes, though they can stay high along the diagonals far from the data, and they are fairly uniform within the middle, random cluster. This is because EquineGP explicitly leverages distances in the embedding space. These distances can also be used to calculate a normalized predictive entropy, which can then be forwarded to the user through the predict() method.

docs.title: EQUINE Toy Problem Example¶
docs.text:
The intent of this example notebook is to provide an easy-to-visualize, 2-D, toy problem that illustrates both the general problem of uncertainty quantification in neural network classification as well as to show how EQUINE can be used to make predictions more robust in the face of uncertainty.

Here, we use the EquineGP class to demonstrate the ideas. This class follows the approach used in Spectral-normalized Neural Gaussian Processes (SNGP), which appends random Fourier features and a Laplace approximation to a Gaussian Process (GP) to the end of a neural network, making it possible to compute out-of-distribution scores (see deterministic uncertainty estimation and the SNGP tutorial). Note that EQUINE does not assume that the user is enforcing a spectral normalization in the neural network embedding, so the results may vary.

This notebook requires some extra dependencies to run. You can uncomment the below cell to install them into your local environment.

docs.title: Generate Toy Dataset¶
docs.text:
This dataset uses make_blobs from scikit-learn, placing 4 clusters in each quadrant (for 4 classes), along with a middle cluster with random class memberships.

In this toy problem, the accuracy should not be much higher than 80%, since the middle class memberships are essentially random.

Additionally, the class confidence in the middle of the problem should hover around 25% for the same reason.

docs.title: Define a feature embedding model¶
docs.text:
Here we define a "usual", sequential neural network architecture, leaving off only the softmax in the forward function. Here, we've arbitrarily selected 16 as the dimension of the feature embeddings (the penultimate layer), but we're classifying on the 4 output categories from above.

The class is registered with @eq.embedding_architecture, because model.save() stores an embedding model as the name of a registered architecture plus its plain-valued constructor arguments and weights (rather than as executable code), and refuses a class that is not registered.

docs.title: Visualizing the Neural Network Uncertainty¶
docs.text: Before continuing onto how EQUINE can help, here's how well the "vanilla" Neural Network does on this problem. Using the above function, we can show the output predictions on the held-out test data and on a uniform grid.

docs.title: Wrapping the Vanilla NN Feature Embedding in EQUINE¶
docs.text:
At first glance, the network is performing very well: it is getting more than 80% accuracy and is very confident about its predictions (the maximum probability is nearly 1.0 almost everywhere). However, the confidence contours reveal that the model is extremely confident everywhere except for a relatively thin boundary between the classes on the x/y axes and in the interior, random cluster. On the held-out test data, the calibration error for this simple problem is also decent.

Next, let's consider all but the last layer of the above neural network as a "feature embedding". In this example, we use EquineGP, which is based upon Spectral Norm Gaussian Processes (for more background, checkout this TensorFlow tutorial as well as the PyTorch reimplementation).

To wrap the feature embedding into an Equine GP, we wrap the embedding model into an EquineGP class:

docs.title: Out of Distribution Indicators¶
docs.text:
EQUINE introduces the predict() method to return predictions with the probability contexts, including

  • classes: the class probabilities
  • ood_scores: the out-of-distribution scores

docs.title: Adding an out-of-distribution class¶
docs.text: Finally, we illustrate the binary predictive performance on "correct" and "incorrect" predictions that would come from using the OOD scores to screen out predictions on likely OOD data.

def calculate_features(row):
    forward_backward_mask = np.array(row.directions, dtype=bool)
    ts = np.array(row.timestamps)
    duration = ts[-1]-ts[0]

    # split out "forward" and "backward" timestamps
    ts_forward = ts[forward_backward_mask] 
    ts_backward = ts[~forward_backward_mask]

    # Bail out if this connection is too short or has very little data
    if duration < 30.0 or len(ts_forward) < 10 or len(ts_backward) < 10:
        return tuple(16*[pd.NA])

    # Statistics for forward interarrival times
    forward_interarrivals = ts_forward[1:]-ts_forward[:-1]
    fiat_mean = np.mean(forward_interarrivals)
    fiat_std = np.std(forward_interarrivals)
    fiat_max = np.max(forward_interarrivals)
    fiat_min = np.min(forward_interarrivals)

    # Statistics for backward interarrival times
    backward_interarrivals = ts_backward[1:]-ts_backward[:-1]
    biat_mean = np.mean(backward_interarrivals)
    biat_std = np.std(backward_interarrivals)
    biat_max = np.max(backward_interarrivals)
    biat_min = np.min(backward_interarrivals)

    # Size statisticstics 
    sizes = np.array(row.sizes)
    total_forward = len(ts_forward)
    total_backward = len(ts_backward)
    bytes_forward = sum(sizes[forward_backward_mask])
    bytes_backward = sum(sizes[~forward_backward_mask])
    bytes_per_sec = (bytes_forward + bytes_backward) / duration
    num_unique_forward_sizes = len(np.unique(sizes[forward_backward_mask]))
    num_unique_backward_sizes = len(np.unique(sizes[~forward_backward_mask]))

    return  (duration, fiat_mean, fiat_std, fiat_max, fiat_min, 
            biat_mean, biat_std, biat_max, biat_min, 
            total_forward, total_backward, 
            bytes_forward, bytes_backward, bytes_per_sec, 
            num_unique_forward_sizes, num_unique_backward_sizes)
def calculate_features(row): forward_backward_mask = np.array(row.directions, dtype=bool) ts = np.array(row.timestamps) duration = ts[-1]-ts[0] # split out "forward" and "backward" timestamps ts_forward = ts[forward_backward_mask] ts_backward = ts[~forward_backward_mask] # Bail out if this connection is too short or has very little data if duration < 30.0 or len(ts_forward) < 10 or len(ts_backward) < 10: return tuple(16*[pd.NA]) # Statistics for forward interarrival times forward_interarrivals = ts_forward[1:]-ts_forward[:-1] fiat_mean = np.mean(forward_interarrivals) fiat_std = np.std(forward_interarrivals) fiat_max = np.max(forward_interarrivals) fiat_min = np.min(forward_interarrivals) # Statistics for backward interarrival times backward_interarrivals = ts_backward[1:]-ts_backward[:-1] biat_mean = np.mean(backward_interarrivals) biat_std = np.std(backward_interarrivals) biat_max = np.max(backward_interarrivals) biat_min = np.min(backward_interarrivals) # Size statisticstics sizes = np.array(row.sizes) total_forward = len(ts_forward) total_backward = len(ts_backward) bytes_forward = sum(sizes[forward_backward_mask]) bytes_backward = sum(sizes[~forward_backward_mask]) bytes_per_sec = (bytes_forward + bytes_backward) / duration num_unique_forward_sizes = len(np.unique(sizes[forward_backward_mask])) num_unique_backward_sizes = len(np.unique(sizes[~forward_backward_mask])) return (duration, fiat_mean, fiat_std, fiat_max, fiat_min, biat_mean, biat_std, biat_max, biat_min, total_forward, total_backward, bytes_forward, bytes_backward, bytes_per_sec, num_unique_forward_sizes, num_unique_backward_sizes) In [7]: Copied!

@eq.embedding_architecture("examples.vnat_embedding")
class EmbeddingModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, num_deep_features):
        super(EmbeddingModel, self).__init__()
        # The normalization statistics are buffers, so they are saved with the
        # weights; set_normalization() fills them in after construction
        self.register_buffer("train_means", torch.zeros(1, input_dim))
        self.register_buffer("train_deviations", torch.ones(1, input_dim))
        self.linear_relu_stack = torch.nn.Sequential(
            torch.nn.Linear(input_dim, num_deep_features),
            torch.nn.ReLU(),
            torch.nn.Linear(num_deep_features, num_deep_features),
            torch.nn.ReLU(),
            torch.nn.Linear(num_deep_features, num_deep_features),
            torch.nn.ReLU(),
            torch.nn.Linear(num_deep_features, num_deep_features),
        )

    def set_normalization(self, train_means, train_deviations):
        with torch.no_grad():
            self.train_means.copy_(train_means)
            self.train_deviations.copy_(train_deviations)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = (x - self.train_means ) / self.train_deviations
        logits = self.linear_relu_stack(x)
        return logits

docs.title: EQUINE Example on VPN/NonVPN Network Application Traffic Dataset (VNAT)¶
docs.text:
This example showcases how to use an EQUINE class to analyze an encrypted network traffic dataset. The general question of interest from this dataset is whether it is possible to discern the application that generated network traffic, even if that traffic is routed through a Virtual Private Network (VPN). To try this example out, you will need to download the connections dataframe from that location and place it in the same directory as this notebook. For more information, check out this paper in the IEEE Journal, Transactions of Artificial Intelligence.

In this example, we'll demonstrate how to add labels and features to the dataframe and then train an EquineProtonet model, holding out two of the five classes, in order to evaluate its performance at assigning relatively high out-of-distribution scores for the two held-out classes.

docs.title: Dataset Preparation¶
docs.text: We'll use pandas to read the HDF5 file. It should produce a dataframe with the keys "connection", "timestamps", "sizes", "directions" and "file_names".

docs.title: Feature Generation¶
docs.text: Next, we'll generate some simple "transport layer statistics" to use as classification features. Essentially, these are statistical features calculated over the entirety of each connection, including things like the average "interarrival times" between packets, the total amount of bytes transferred, etc. Note that the below code filters any connections with fewer than 10 packets in either direction or shorter than 30 seconds.

docs.title: Grouped Data Characteristics¶
docs.text: Note here that we have grouped only by application type. Since there are few remaining single-connection examples of file-transfer and VOIP, we'll hold those out for out-of-distribution testing.

docs.title: Create an Embedding Model and train a Neural Network¶
docs.text:
We next create a simple embedding model that we'll use to train from scratch using the train_episodes method in EquineProtonet. Given that the predictions are on the entire connnections (and some of them are pretty long), this is not too challenging a prediction problem, even though some of the connections are tunnneled through a VPN. This is because the size and timing characteristics of the connections are not always obscured by VPNs.

The class is registered with @eq.embedding_architecture, because model.save() stores an embedding model as the name of a registered architecture plus its plain-valued constructor arguments and weights (rather than as executable code), and refuses a class that is not registered. So its constructor takes only sizes, and the training-set normalization statistics are buffers (saved with the weights) that are filled in after construction.

docs.title: Train a model¶
docs.text: Here we create the Neural Network from scratch using the above feature embedding model and perform episodic training. Other examples showcase how one can pretrain and freeze layers in the feature embedding model, but for this example, we simply train from scratch, which should only take a few seconds on a CPU.

docs.title: Out of distribution study¶
docs.text: Here we demonstrate that the remaining two application categories, VOIP and File Transfer (FT), which were not included in the model training, produce relatively high out-of-distribution, represented by the ood_scores in EquineOutput. In the below cell, we consider the held-out test data as in-distribution for reference, whereas the VOIP and FT connections are the ood_data. To generate a ROC curve, we concatenate the test and OOD data together and use the ood_scores as a signifier as to whether they were in- or out-of-distribution. The histogram should reveal thaat the majority of the OOD data is in the highest scoring bin (closest to 1.0).

class Equine(torch.nn.Module, ABC):
    """EQUINE Abstract Base Class (ABC):
    EQUINE is set up to extend torch's nn.Module to enrich it with
    a method that enables uncertainty quantification and visualization. Most
    importantly, the `.predict()` method must be outfitted to return an
    EquineOutput object that contains both the class probabilities
    *and* an out-of-distribution (ood) score.

    Parameters
    ----------
    embedding_model : torch.nn.Module
        The embedding model to use.
    head_layers : int, optional
        The number of layers to use in the model head, by default 1.
    device : str, optional
        The device to train the equine model on (defaults to cpu).
    feature_names : list[str], optional
        List of strings of the names of the tabular features (ex ["duration", "fiat_mean", ...])
    label_names : list[str], optional
        List of strings of the names of the labels (ex ["streaming", "voip", ...])

    Attributes
    ----------
    device : str
        The device to train the equine model on (defaults to cpu).
    embedding_model : torch.nn.Module
        The neural embedding model to enrich with uncertainty quantification.
    feature_names : list[str], optional
        List of strings of the names of the tabular features (ex ["duration", "fiat_mean", ...])
    head_layers : int
        The number of linear layers to append to the embedding model (default 1, not always used).
    label_names : list[str], optional
        List of strings of the names of the labels (ex ["streaming", "voip", ...])
    train_summary : dict[str, Any]
        A dictionary containing information about the model training.

    Raises
    ------
    NotImplementedError
        If any of the abstract methods are not implemented.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        embedding_model: torch.nn.Module,
        head_layers: int = 1,
        device: str = "cpu",
        feature_names: list[str] | None = None,
        label_names: list[str] | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding_model = embedding_model
        self.head_layers = head_layers
        self.train_summary: dict[str, Any] = {
            "numTrainExamples": 0,
            "dateTrained": "",
            "modelType": "",
        }
        self.device = device
        self.to(device)
        self.embedding_model.to(device)
        self.feature_names = feature_names
        self.label_names = label_names

    def _apply(
        self, fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor], recurse: bool = True
    ) -> "Equine":
        """
        ``nn.Module._apply``, extended to the stored tensors listed in
        ``_apply_to_stored_tensors``.

        ``to``, ``cpu``, ``cuda`` and the dtype casts call it. ``model.to(device)``
        moves every tensor the model keeps and updates ``device`` (see
        ``_apply_to_stored_tensors``).
        """
        super()._apply(fn, recurse)
        _apply_to_stored_tensors(self, fn, recurse)
        return self

    @abstractmethod
    def forward(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Forward pass of the model. This is to preserve the usual behavior
        of torch.nn.Module.

        Parameters
        ----------
        X : torch.Tensor
            The input data.

        Returns
        -------
        torch.Tensor
            The output of the model.

        """
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    def predict(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> EquineOutput:
        """
        Upon implementation, predicts the class probabilities and out-of-distribution (ood) scores for the
        given input data.

        Parameters
        ----------
        X : torch.Tensor
            The input data.

        Returns
        -------
        EquineOutput
            An EquineOutput object containing the class probabilities and OOD scores.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    def train_model(
        self, dataset: TensorDataset, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """
        Upon implementation, train the model on the given dataset.

        Parameters
        ----------
        dataset : TensorDataset
            TensorDataset containing the training data.
        **kwargs
            Additional keyword arguments to pass to the training function.

        Returns
        -------
        dict[str, Any]
            Dictionary containing summary training information and any other data
            Note that at least one key should be 'train_summary'
        """
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    def update_support(
        self,
        support_x: torch.Tensor,
        support_y: torch.Tensor,
        *args: Any,
        **kwargs: Any,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Upon implementation, replace the model's support with examples taken from
        the given ones.

        Parameters
        ----------
        support_x : torch.Tensor
            Tensor containing the examples to take the support from.
        support_y : torch.Tensor
            Tensor containing the label of each example in ``support_x``.
        *args, **kwargs
            The options of the implementation: ``calib_frac`` and ``label_names``
            for ``EquineProtonet``, ``support_size`` for ``EquineGP``, each passed
            by keyword.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    def get_support(self) -> OrderedDict[int, torch.Tensor]:
        """
        Upon implementation, returns the support examples.

        Returns
        -------
        OrderedDict[int, torch.Tensor]
            The support examples of each class, keyed by label.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    def get_prototypes(self) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Upon implementation, returns the prototype embeddings

        Returns
        -------
        torch.Tensor
            A torch tensor of the prototype embeddings
        """
        raise NotImplementedError

    @abstractmethod
    def save(self, path: str) -> None:
        """
        Upon implementation, save the model to the given file path.

        Parameters
        ----------
        path : str
            File path to save the model to.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError

    @classmethod  # type: ignore
    def load(cls: AnyEquine, path: str) -> AnyEquine:  # noqa: F821 # type: ignore
        """
        Upon implementation, load the model from the given file path.

        Parameters
        ----------
        path : str
            File path to load the model from.

        Returns
        -------
        Equine
            Loaded model object.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError

    def get_label_names(self) -> list[str] | None:
        """
        Retrieve the label names used in the model.

        Returns
        -------
        list[str] | None
            A list of label names if available; otherwise, None.
        """
        if hasattr(self, "label_names"):
            return self.label_names
        return None

    def _label_order(self) -> list[int] | None:
        """
        The class label of each column of ``predict``'s ``classes``.

        Returns
        -------
        list[int] | None
            None: column ``j`` holds label ``j``.
        """
        return None

    def get_feature_names(self) -> list[str] | None:
        """
        Retrieve the feature names used in the model.

        Returns
        -------
        list[str] | None
            A list of feature names if available; otherwise, None.
        """
        if hasattr(self, "feature_names"):
            return self.feature_names
        return None

    @icontract.require(
        lambda num_features, num_classes: num_features > 0 and num_classes > 0
    )
    def validate_feature_label_names(self, num_features: int, num_classes: int) -> None:
        """
        Validate that the feature names and label names, if provided, match the expected counts.

        Parameters
        ----------
        num_features : int
            The expected number of features.
        num_classes : int
            The expected number of classes.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If the length of `feature_names` does not match `num_features`, or
            if the length of `label_names` does not match `num_classes`.
        """

        if feature_names is not None and len(feature_names) != num_features:
            raise ValueError(
                f"The length of feature_names ({len(feature_names)}) does not match the number of data features ({num_features}). Update feature_names or set feature_names to None."
            )

        label_names = self.get_label_names()
        if label_names is not None and len(label_names) != num_classes:
            raise ValueError(
                f"The length of label_names ({len(label_names)}) does not match the number of classes ({num_classes}). Update label_names or set label_names to None."
            )

Bases: Equine

An example of an EQUINE model that builds upon the approach in "Spectral Norm Gaussian Processes" (SNGP). This wraps any pytorch embedding neural network and provides the forward, predict, save, and load methods required by Equine.

Notes

Although this model build upon the approach in SNGP, it does not enforce the spectral normalization and ResNet architecture required for SNGP. Instead, it is a simple wrapper around any pytorch embedding neural network. Your mileage may vary.

Source code in src/equine/equine_gp.py 
@beartype
class EquineGP(Equine):
    """
    An example of an EQUINE model that builds upon the approach in "Spectral Norm
    Gaussian Processes" (SNGP). This wraps any pytorch embedding neural network and provides
    the `forward`, `predict`, `save`, and `load` methods required by Equine.

    Notes
    -----
    Although this model build upon the approach in SNGP, it does not enforce the spectral normalization
    and ResNet architecture required for SNGP. Instead, it is a simple wrapper around
    any pytorch embedding neural network. Your mileage may vary.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        embedding_model: torch.nn.Module,
        emb_out_dim: int,
        num_classes: int,
        num_random_features: int = _DEFAULT_NUM_RANDOM_FEATURES,
        init_temperature: float = 1.0,
        device: str = "cpu",
        feature_names: list[str] | None = None,
        label_names: list[str] | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Initialize the EquineGP model.

        Parameters
        ----------
        embedding_model : torch.nn.Module
            Neural Network feature embedding.
        emb_out_dim : int
            The number of deep features from the feature embedding.
        num_classes : int
            The number of output classes this model predicts.
        num_random_features : int
            The dimension of the output of the RandomFourierFeatures operation
        init_temperature : float, optional
            What to use as the initial temperature (1.0 has no effect).
        device : str, optional
            The device to train the equine model on ('cpu', 'cuda' or 'mps';
            defaults to cpu).
        feature_names : list[str], optional
            List of strings of the names of the tabular features (ex ["duration", "fiat_mean", ...])
        label_names : list[str], optional
            List of strings of the names of the labels (ex ["streaming", "voip", ...])

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If ``emb_out_dim``, ``num_classes`` or ``num_random_features`` is
            not a positive integer.
        """
        _positive_int(emb_out_dim, "emb_out_dim")
        _positive_int(num_classes, "num_classes")
        _positive_int(num_random_features, "num_random_features")
        super().__init__(
            embedding_model,
            device=device,
            feature_names=feature_names,
            label_names=label_names,
        )
        self.support: OrderedDict[int, torch.Tensor] = OrderedDict()
        self.support_embeddings: OrderedDict[int, torch.Tensor] = OrderedDict()
        self.prototypes: torch.Tensor = torch.Tensor()
        self.num_deep_features = emb_out_dim
        self.num_gp_features = emb_out_dim
        self.normalize_gp_features = True
        self.num_random_features = num_random_features
        self.num_outputs = num_classes
        self.mean_field_factor = 25
        self.ridge_penalty = 1
        self.feature_scale: float = 2.0
        self.init_temperature = init_temperature
        self.register_buffer(
            "temperature", torch.Tensor(self.init_temperature * torch.ones(1))
        )
        self.model: _Laplace = _Laplace(
            self.embedding_model,
            self.num_deep_features,
            self.num_gp_features,
            self.normalize_gp_features,
            self.num_random_features,
            self.num_outputs,
            self.feature_scale,
            self.mean_field_factor,
            self.ridge_penalty,
        )
        # Moves the temperature buffer and the Laplace head onto the model's device.
        self.to(self.device)

    @property
    def device_type(self) -> str:
        """Deprecated alias of ``device``."""
        warnings.warn(
            _DEVICE_TYPE_DEPRECATION,
            DeprecationWarning,
            # Past the beartype wrapper (none under -O), to the caller's line.
            stacklevel=2 + (0 if sys.flags.optimize else 1),
        )
        return self.device

    @device_type.setter
    def device_type(self, value: str) -> None:
        """
        Deprecated: moves the model with ``model.to(value)``, then assigns ``device``.
        """
        warnings.warn(
            _DEVICE_TYPE_DEPRECATION,
            DeprecationWarning,
            # Past nn.Module.__setattr__ and the beartype wrapper (none under -O).
            stacklevel=3 + (0 if sys.flags.optimize else 1),
        )
        # The module moves before ``device`` changes.
        self.to(value)
        self.device = value

    def train_model(
        self,
        dataset: Dataset,
        loss_fn: Callable,
        opt: torch.optim.Optimizer,
        num_epochs: int,
        scheduler: torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LRScheduler | None = None,
        batch_size: int = 64,
        validation_dataset: Dataset | None = None,
        val_metrics: Iterable[Metric] | None = None,
        vis_support: bool = False,
        support_size: int = 25,
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """
        Train or fine-tune an EquineGP model.

        Parameters
        ----------
        dataset : Dataset
            The training data. ``dataset[:]`` must return the ``(inputs, labels)``
            tensors, as it does for a ``TensorDataset``, a ``Subset`` of one or a
            part returned by ``random_split``. ``vis_support=True`` needs a
            ``TensorDataset`` (``dataset.tensors``).
        loss_fn : Callable
            A pytorch loss function, e.g., torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss().
        opt : torch.optim.Optimizer
            A pytorch optimizer, e.g., torch.optim.Adam().
        num_epochs : int
            The desired number of epochs to use for training.
        scheduler : torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LRScheduler, optional
            A pytorch scheduler, stepped once after each epoch's training pass.
        validation_dataset: Dataset
            If provided, will compute validation metrics on this dataset after each epoch of training
        val_metrics : Iterable[Metric], optional
            torchmetrics metrics computed on ``validation_dataset`` after each
            epoch. Each one is moved to this model's device in place and reset
            before each epoch's validation pass.
        batch_size : int, optional
            The number of samples to use per batch.
        vis_support : bool, optional
            If True, calls ``update_support`` with the training tensors after the
            last epoch. Requires a ``TensorDataset``.
        support_size : int, optional
            Maximum number of support examples per class that ``update_support``
            keeps when ``vis_support`` is True.

        Returns
        -------
        dict[str, Any]
            ``{"train_summary": ...}`` (the dict ``generate_train_summary``
            builds, also stored on ``self.train_summary``) plus, when a
            ``validation_dataset`` was given, ``"val_metrics"``: one list per
            metric in ``val_metrics`` holding what its ``compute()`` returned
            after each epoch, usually a tensor (``None`` when ``val_metrics``
            was not given). The entry for epoch ``n`` covers that epoch's
            validation pass only.

        Notes
        -----
        Training and eval mode are toggled on this wrapper, which propagates to the
        inner module. The model is left in eval mode afterwards, ready to predict.
        """

        self.validate_feature_label_names(dataset[0][0].shape[-1], self.num_outputs)

        train_loader = DataLoader(
            dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True, drop_last=False
        )

        val_loader: DataLoader | None = None
        if validation_dataset is not None:
            val_loader = DataLoader(
                validation_dataset,
                batch_size=batch_size,
                shuffle=False,
                drop_last=False,
            )

        self.model.set_training_params(len(dataset), batch_size)
        val_metrics_outputs: list[list[Any]] | None = None

        if validation_dataset is not None and val_metrics is not None:
            val_metrics = list(val_metrics)
            for metric in val_metrics:
                metric.to(self.device)
            val_metrics_outputs = [[] for _ in val_metrics]

        for _ in tqdm(range(num_epochs)):
            self.train()  # wrapper and inner module together
            self.model.reset_precision_matrix()
            epoch_loss = 0.0
            for i, (xs, labels) in enumerate(train_loader):
                opt.zero_grad()
                xs = self._input_to_model(xs)
                labels = labels.to(self.device)
                yhats = self.model(xs)
                loss = loss_fn(yhats, labels.to(torch.long))
                loss.backward()
                opt.step()
                epoch_loss += loss.item()
            if scheduler is not None:
                scheduler.step()
            self.eval()
            # compute the validation metrics
            if (
                validation_dataset is not None
                and val_loader is not None
                and val_metrics is not None
                and val_metrics_outputs is not None
            ):
                for metric in val_metrics:
                    metric.reset()
                for _, (xs_val, labels_val) in enumerate(val_loader):
                    xs_val = self._input_to_model(xs_val)
                    labels_val = labels_val.to(self.device)
                    yhats_val = self.model(xs_val)
                    for metric in val_metrics:
                        metric.update(yhats_val, labels_val)
                for i, metric in enumerate(val_metrics):
                    val_metrics_outputs[i].append(metric.compute())
        if vis_support:
            self.update_support(
                dataset.tensors[0], dataset.tensors[1], support_size=support_size
            )

        _, train_y = dataset[:]
        date_trained = datetime.now().strftime("%m/%d/%Y, %H:%M:%S")
        self.train_summary: dict[str, Any] = generate_train_summary(
            self, train_y, date_trained
        )

        return_dict: dict[str, Any] = dict()
        return_dict["train_summary"] = self.train_summary
        if validation_dataset is not None:
            return_dict["val_metrics"] = val_metrics_outputs

        return return_dict

    def update_support(
        self,
        support_x: torch.Tensor,
        support_y: torch.Tensor,
        *args: Any,
        support_size: int | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        """Replace the support with up to ``support_size`` examples of each class,
        and store their embeddings and the class prototypes.

        Computes in eval mode and leaves the model in the mode the caller had it in (via
        ``train()``/``eval()``).

        Parameters
        ----------
        support_x : torch.Tensor
            Tensor containing the examples to take the support from.
        support_y : torch.Tensor
            Tensor containing the label of each example in ``support_x``.
        *args : Any
            Deprecated: ``support_size`` passed by position. Emits a
            ``DeprecationWarning`` and is then handled as the keyword.
        support_size : int
            Maximum number of support examples to keep per class. Required,
            keyword-only.

        Returns
        -------
        None

        Raises
        ------
        TypeError
            If ``support_size`` is missing, is passed both by position and by
            keyword, or more than one option is passed by position.
        ValueError
            If ``support_x`` and ``support_y`` hold different numbers of examples.
        """
        if len(args) > 1:
            raise TypeError(
                "EquineGP.update_support() takes at most 1 option by position "
                f"(support_size) but {len(args)} were given"
            )
        if args:
            if support_size is not None:
                raise TypeError(
                    "EquineGP.update_support() got multiple values for argument "
                    "'support_size'"
                )
            warnings.warn(
                "Passing support_size to EquineGP.update_support by position is "
                "deprecated and will stop working in the next release: pass "
                "support_size=... by keyword.",
                DeprecationWarning,
                # Past the beartype wrapper (none under -O), to the caller's line.
                stacklevel=2 + (0 if sys.flags.optimize else 1),
            )
            EquineGP.update_support(self, support_x, support_y, support_size=args[0])
            return
        if support_size is None:
            raise TypeError(
                "EquineGP.update_support() missing required keyword argument: "
                "'support_size'"
            )
        with _eval_mode(self):
            if support_x.shape[0] != support_y.shape[0]:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"support_x has {support_x.shape[0]} examples but support_y has "
                    f"{support_y.shape[0]} labels; they must match."
                )
            labels, counts = torch.unique(support_y, return_counts=True)
            shuffled_idxs = _get_shuffle_idxs_by_class(support_y, labels.tolist())
            support = OrderedDict()
            for label, count in list(zip(labels.tolist(), counts.tolist())):
                class_support = generate_support(
                    support_x,
                    support_y,
                    support_size=min(count, support_size),
                    selected_labels=[label],
                    shuffled_indexes={label: shuffled_idxs[label]},
                )
                support.update(class_support)

            # Through the model boundary: on the device and, for floating support, in
            # the model's dtype.
            self.support = OrderedDict(
                (label, self._input_to_model(x)) for label, x in support.items()
            )

            # Embedded without autograd: the result carries no graph.
            with torch.no_grad():
                support_embeddings = OrderedDict().fromkeys(
                    self.support.keys(), torch.Tensor()
                )
                for label in self.support:
                    support_embeddings[label] = self.compute_embeddings(
                        self.support[label]
                    )

                self.support_embeddings = support_embeddings
                self.prototypes = self._prototypes_from_embeddings()

    def compute_embeddings(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Method for computing deep embeddings for given input tensor.

        Parameters
        ----------
        x : torch.Tensor
            Input tensor for generating embeddings.

        Returns
        -------
        torch.Tensor
            Output embeddings .
        """
        x = self._input_to_model(x)
        f = self.model.feature_extractor(x)
        f_reduc = self.model.jl(f)
        if self.model.normalize_gp_features:
            f_reduc = self.model.normalize(f_reduc)

        return self.model.rff(f_reduc)

    @icontract.require(lambda self: len(self.support) > 0)
    def compute_prototypes(self) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Method for computing class prototypes based on given support examples.
        ``Prototypes'' in this context are the means of the support embeddings for each class.

        Embeds ``self.support`` with the current model (one pass per class)
        and returns the mean of each class's embeddings, in support order.
        Nothing is stored: ``support_embeddings`` and ``prototypes`` are left
        as they are.

        Returns
        -------
        torch.Tensor
            Tensors of prototypes for each of the given classes in the support.
        """
        embeddings = [self.compute_embeddings(x) for x in self.support.values()]
        return torch.stack([torch.mean(e, dim=0) for e in embeddings])

    @icontract.require(lambda self: len(self.support_embeddings) > 0)
    def _prototypes_from_embeddings(self) -> torch.Tensor:
        """Mean of ``self.support_embeddings`` per class, in support order; embeds nothing."""
        proto_list = []
        for label in self.support_embeddings:  # look at doing functorch
            class_prototype = torch.mean(self.support_embeddings[label], dim=0)
            proto_list.append(class_prototype)

        prototypes = torch.stack(proto_list)

        return prototypes

    @icontract.require(lambda self: len(self.support) > 0)
    def get_support(self) -> OrderedDict[int, torch.Tensor]:
        """
        Method for returning support examples used in training.

        Returns
        -------
        OrderedDict[int, torch.Tensor]
            Dictionary containing support examples for each class.
        """
        return self.support

    @icontract.require(lambda self: len(self.prototypes) > 0)
    def get_prototypes(self) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Method for returning class prototypes.

        Returns
        -------
        torch.Tensor
            Tensors of prototypes for each of the given classes in the support.
        """
        return self.prototypes

    @icontract.require(lambda num_calibration_epochs: 0 < num_calibration_epochs)
    @icontract.require(lambda calibration_lr: calibration_lr > 0.0)
    def calibrate_model(
        self,
        dataset: torch.utils.data.Dataset,
        num_calibration_epochs: int = 1,
        calibration_lr: float = 0.01,
        calibration_batch_size: int = 256,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Fine-tune the temperature on ``dataset``.

        ``train_model`` does not call this method; ``temperature`` stays at
        ``init_temperature`` until it is called.

        Parameters
        ----------
        dataset : Dataset
            A map-style pytorch ``Dataset`` (with ``__len__``) of
            ``(input, label)`` pairs.
        num_calibration_epochs : int, optional
            Number of epochs to tune temperature.
        calibration_lr : float, optional
            Learning rate for temperature optimization.
        calibration_batch_size : int, optional
            Batch size of the calibration data loader.
        """

        calibration_loader = DataLoader(
            dataset,
            batch_size=calibration_batch_size,
            shuffle=True,
            drop_last=False,
        )

        self.temperature.requires_grad = True
        loss_fn = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy
        optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([self.temperature], lr=calibration_lr)
        for _ in range(num_calibration_epochs):
            for xs, labels in calibration_loader:
                optimizer.zero_grad()
                xs = self._input_to_model(xs)
                labels = labels.to(self.device)
                with torch.no_grad():
                    logits = self.model(xs)
                logits = logits / self.temperature
                loss = loss_fn(logits, labels.to(torch.long))
                loss.backward()
                optimizer.step()
        self.temperature.requires_grad = False

    def _input_to_model(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Move ``X`` to the model device; a floating input is cast to the model's dtype.

        The reference is the Laplace head (``self.model``, see
        ``utils._input_to_model``): its first parameter is the embedding
        model's when that has one, else the head's own (``normalize.weight`` or
        ``beta``). A parameter-less embedding such as ``nn.Identity`` gets an input in
        the head's dtype.
        """
        return _input_to_model(X, self.model, self.device)

    def forward(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        EquineGP forward function, generates logits for classification.

        Parameters
        ----------
        X : torch.Tensor
            Input tensor for generating predictions. Moved to the model device
            and cast to the embedding model's parameter dtype.

        Returns
        -------
        torch.Tensor
            Logits divided by ``temperature``, shape (examples, classes).
        """
        logits, _ = self._forward_with_embeddings(X)
        return logits

    def _forward_with_embeddings(
        self, X: torch.Tensor
    ) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
        """
        ``forward`` that also returns its embeddings.

        The embeddings are ``compute_embeddings(X)``, with a single unbatched
        example given a batch dimension of one.
        """
        X = self._input_to_model(X)
        logits, embeddings = self.model._forward_with_features(X)
        logits = cast(torch.Tensor, logits)  # mean_field_factor is always set
        temperature = cast(torch.Tensor, self.temperature)  # registered buffer
        return logits / temperature, embeddings

    @icontract.ensure(
        lambda result: all((0 <= result.ood_scores) & (result.ood_scores <= 1.0))
    )
    def predict(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> EquineOutput:
        """
        Predict function for EquineGP, inherited and implemented from Equine.

        Computes in eval mode and leaves the model in the mode the caller had it in (via
        ``train()``/``eval()``). Every submodule's mode is restored; an embedding frozen
        with ``model.embedding_model.eval()`` during fine-tuning stays frozen.

        Parameters
        ----------
        X : torch.Tensor
            Input tensor. It is moved to the model device and cast to the embedding
            model's parameter dtype; a float64 input to a float32 model is accepted.

        Returns
        -------
        EquineOutput
            Output object containing prediction probabilities, OOD scores and
            embeddings. Computed under ``torch.no_grad()``: the tensors carry
            no autograd graph but are ordinary tensors (not inference-mode
            tensors), which a caller can use in autograd.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If ``X`` is empty, or its embeddings hold a NaN or infinite value.
        """
        _require_examples(X)
        # One embedding pass, under no_grad.
        with _eval_mode(self), torch.no_grad():
            logits, embeddings = self._forward_with_embeddings(X)
            _require_finite_embeddings(embeddings)
            preds = torch.softmax(logits, dim=1)
            equiprobable = (
                torch.ones(self.num_outputs, device=logits.device) / self.num_outputs
            )
            max_entropy = torch.sum(torch.special.entr(equiprobable))
            ood_score = torch.sum(torch.special.entr(preds), dim=1) / max_entropy
        eq_out = EquineOutput(
            classes=preds, ood_scores=ood_score, embeddings=embeddings
        )

        self.validate_feature_label_names(X.shape[-1], self.num_outputs)

        return eq_out

    def save(self, path: str) -> None:
        """
        Save all model parameters to a file.

        The embedding model (the feature extractor) is stored as a *recipe*
        (registered architecture name plus constructor arguments) and a
        ``state_dict``, so the file holds only data.

        Parameters
        ----------
        path : str
            Filename to write the model.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If the embedding model is not a registered architecture.
        RuntimeError
            If the model has not been trained with ``train_model``.
        """
        if self.model.num_data == 0:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "The model has not been trained; call train_model before save."
            )
        torch.save(self._to_checkpoint(), path)

    def _to_checkpoint(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Build the checkpoint dictionary that ``save`` writes and ``_from_checkpoint`` reads."""
        model_settings = {
            "emb_out_dim": self.num_deep_features,
            "num_classes": self.num_outputs,
            "num_random_features": self.num_random_features,
            "init_temperature": self.temperature.item(),
            "device": self.device,
        }
        # The feature extractor is the embedding model, stored separately.
        laplace_sd = {
            key: value
            for key, value in self.model.state_dict().items()
            if "feature_extractor" not in key
        }
        # Plain values only, so load_checkpoint can read it with weights_only=True.
        save_data: dict[str, Any] = {
            "equine_format_version": EQUINE_FORMAT_VERSION,
            **_embedding_checkpoint(self.embedding_model),
            "feature_names": _plain_names(self.feature_names),
            "label_names": _plain_names(self.label_names),
            "laplace_model_save": laplace_sd,
            "num_data": self.model.num_data,
            "settings": model_settings,
            "support": {
                int(label): x.detach().clone() for label, x in self.support.items()
            },
            "train_batch_size": self.model.train_batch_size,
            "train_summary": _plain_train_summary(self.train_summary),
        }
        return save_data

    @classmethod
    def load(
        cls,
        path: str,
        device: str | None = None,
        *,
        embedding_model: torch.nn.Module | None = None,
    ) -> Equine:
        """
        Load a previously saved EquineGP model.

        Loading runs no code from the file: it is read with
        ``torch.load(weights_only=True)`` and the embedding model is rebuilt from its
        recipe through the architecture registry.

        Parameters
        ----------
        path : str
            Input filename.
        device : str | None
            The device to load the model onto. Overrides the device recorded
            in the file; by default the model lands on the saved device.
        embedding_model : torch.nn.Module | None
            Keyword-only. Use this module as the embedding architecture instead
            of rebuilding it from the file's recipe; the file's weights are
            loaded into it, and its floating-point tensors take their stored
            dtypes.

        Returns
        -------
        EquineGP
            The reconstituted EquineGP object.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If the file is not in the current EQUINE format or stores its
            embedding model as TorchScript (both are rewritten once with
            ``python -m equine.upgrade``), or names an unregistered
            architecture. If ``device`` is unavailable here, names an index at
            or above its device count, or lacks a dtype the file holds (float64
            on MPS: load such a file with ``device="cpu"``).
        """
        model_save = _load_checkpoint_for_device(path, device)
        _refuse_torchscript(model_save, path)
        return cls._from_checkpoint(model_save, device, embedding_model=embedding_model)

    @classmethod
    def _from_checkpoint(
        cls,
        model_save: dict[str, Any],
        device: str | None = None,
        embedding_model: torch.nn.Module | None = None,
    ) -> Equine:
        """
        Rebuild an EquineGP from an already-loaded checkpoint dictionary.

        Parameters
        ----------
        model_save : dict[str, Any]
            The dictionary returned by ``utils.load_checkpoint``.
        device : str | None
            Device override for the reconstituted model.
        embedding_model : torch.nn.Module | None
            Use this module as the embedding architecture instead of the file's
            recipe; the file's weights are loaded into it, and its
            floating-point tensors take their stored dtypes.

        Returns
        -------
        EquineGP
            The reconstituted EquineGP object.
        """
        # The embedding is rebuilt first.
        embedding = _rebuild_embedding(model_save, embedding_model)
        _require_entries(
            model_save,
            (
                "settings",
                "support",
                "train_summary",
                "laplace_model_save",
                "num_data",
                "train_batch_size",
            ),
            cls,
        )
        stored_support = _support_from_file(model_save["support"])
        num_data = _positive_int(model_save["num_data"], "Model file's num_data")
        batch_size = _positive_int(
            model_save["train_batch_size"], "Model file's train_batch_size"
        )
        if batch_size > num_data:
            raise ValueError(
                "Model file's train_batch_size is larger than its num_data; the file "
                "is inconsistent or was tampered with."
            )
        for key in ("feature_names", "label_names"):
            _require_names(model_save.get(key), key)
        settings = _checked_settings(cls, model_save["settings"])
        # Allow the user to override the saved device state dynamically
        if device is not None:
            settings["device"] = device
        else:
            _require_device(settings, hint=" (pass device= to choose another)")
        # The stored Laplace weights are checked against the settings before the model
        # is built.
        _require_matching_weights(
            _expected_laplace_state(settings),
            model_save.get("laplace_model_save"),
            "laplace_model_save",
        )
        try:
            eq_model = cls(embedding, **settings)
        except Exception as err:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Could not build {cls.__name__} from the model file's settings "
                f"({_truncate(_describe_error(err), 200)})."
            ) from err

        eq_model.feature_names = model_save.get("feature_names")
        eq_model.label_names = model_save.get("label_names")
        eq_model.train_summary = model_save.get("train_summary")

        _adopt_stored_dtypes(
            eq_model.model, model_save["laplace_model_save"], "laplace_model_save"
        )
        eq_model.model.load_state_dict(
            model_save.get("laplace_model_save"), strict=False
        )
        # The load_state_dict post hook has already updated _seen_count.
        eq_model.model.seen_data = (
            model_save.get("laplace_model_save")
            .get("seen_data")
            .to(eq_model.model.precision.device)
        )

        eq_model.model.set_training_params(
            model_save.get("num_data"), model_save.get("train_batch_size")
        )
        eq_model.eval()

        # load_checkpoint returns CPU tensors; the support goes to the model's device.
        try:
            support = OrderedDict(
                (label, x.to(eq_model.device)) for label, x in stored_support.items()
            )
            if len(support) > 0:
                eq_model.support = support
                with torch.no_grad():
                    eq_model.support_embeddings = OrderedDict(
                        (label, eq_model.compute_embeddings(x))
                        for label, x in support.items()
                    )
                    eq_model.prototypes = eq_model._prototypes_from_embeddings()
        except Exception as err:
            raise ValueError(
                "Model file's support could not be passed through its embedding "
                f"model ({_truncate(_describe_error(err), 200)}); the "
                "file is inconsistent or was tampered with."
            ) from err

        return eq_model
